strengths: Addresses an important and understudied problem: unsafe intermediate reasoning in LRMs that persists despite safe final responses

Provides novel systematic empirical insights: identifies 'safety triggers' via CSR analysis with clear methodology, demonstrates strong correlation (r=0.85) between compliance cues and unsafe continuations
Clear motivation for method design: Section 2.3 effectively diagnoses RL limitations (50% of prompts yield no safe rollouts), motivating the preference optimization approach
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three LRMs, three safety benchmarks, separate reasoning/response safety assessment, utility preservation on four tasks, and over-refusal measurement
Strong empirical results: 82.4% → 23.4% harmful reasoning on WildJailbreak, >30% relative harmfulness reduction, maintained reasoning capabilities, 3.5× faster than GRPO
Thorough analysis with ablations on cue detectors, training algorithm variants, KL divergence visualization, and sampling efficiency comparison
Clear presentation with informative visualizations, well-structured narrative, and practical algorithmic details
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: core contribution applies existing DPO to manually intervened trajectories; the intervention strategy itself (replacing bad steps with good ones) is conceptually straightforward

Critical dependency on external models (GPT-4o): used for compliance cue detection, safety evaluation, and trigger identification, creating circular dependency and reproducibility concerns; while ablations show robustness, they still use external models

Over-refusal not adequately addressed: XsTest compliance rates of 71.2-80.0% indicate substantial over-refusal; second-stage training appears ad-hoc with unclear principled solution to safety-utility trade-off
Limited scale and generalization: only 1,000 harmful prompts yielding 520-1,438 preference pairs; no scaling analysis; only two model families tested; no cross-model transfer analysis
Limited safety trigger pool: only 6 generic triggers used repeatedly with no systematic construction approach, diversity analysis, or domain adaptation strategy
Evaluation limitations: manual annotation only on 100 examples; no adversarial evaluation against detection evasion; GPT-4o as safety evaluator could be gamed by models learning its judgment patterns
Incomplete baseline comparisons: SFT baselines unavailable for Qwen3-8B; missing comparisons with other process supervision methods; GRPO optimization unclear
Missing technical sensitivity analysis: arbitrary CSR thresholds (µ=0.9, K=15) without justification; no convergence analysis for iterative intervention; limited failure mode discussion
Insufficient statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance reporting; 'multiple runs' mentioned but averaging procedure not detailed

Unresolved reasoning capability trade-offs: some task decreases not explained; auxiliary SFT loss coefficient (0.2) suggests potential training instability; limited analysis of modified reasoning patterns

strengths: Addresses important and timely problem of reasoning-level safety in LRMs with well-motivated analysis showing existing aligned models still contain unsafe reasoning
Strong empirical results across multiple models and benchmarks (30%+ relative reduction in harmfulness) with comprehensive evaluation on diverse attack types and harm categories

Novel empirical insights about safety dynamics: systematic identification of safety triggers via CSR analysis, strong compliance cue correlation (r=0.85), and demonstrating corrective interventions work (Figure 6)
Efficient method compared to GRPO: requires ~14 generations vs 40, trains in 40 min vs 2+ hours, with straightforward implementation
Extensive experimental coverage including ablations, scaling studies (1.5B-14B), robustness to obfuscated/paraphrased/adaptive attacks, and generalization to 6 additional benchmarks
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and well-structured analysis of safety-utility tradeoffs
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: core contribution is DPO applied to intervened data (both DPO and preference learning for safety are established); main novelty is data construction strategy based on observational analysis of safety dynamics

Critical reproducibility barrier: heavy reliance on closed-source GPT-4o for both compliance cue detection (83% human agreement) and safety evaluation (93.7% agreement), creating circular dependency that prevents independent reproduction or improvement

Evaluation methodology concerns: primary safety evaluation depends entirely on GPT-4o, human evaluation limited to ~94 outputs on one benchmark, no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals despite claiming multiple runs, small analysis set (30 prompts for CSR analysis)

Safety triggers appear hand-selected (Table 4) rather than systematically extracted; no analysis of linguistic/semantic properties making triggers effective; only 6 generic triggers used with unclear generalization to new domains
Over-refusal not fully resolved: XsTest compliance rates (80% DS-8B, 71.2% DS-7B) substantially higher than several baselines, suggesting two-stage mitigation strategy only partially effective

Data construction choices inadequately justified: N=1 (single intervention) limits diversity with no ablation; filtering for trajectories with no compliance after single replacement may exclude harder cases; hyperparameters (μ=0.9, K=15, η=0.1) lack sensitivity analysis
Incomplete theoretical understanding: reward shaping connection (Section 3.4) lacks formal justification; no analysis of why DPO on intervened trajectories outperforms RL beyond informal arguments

Scope limitations: only jailbreak-style attacks evaluated; single model family (LLaMA/Qwen-based); unclear generalization to other safety violations (hallucinations, benign toxicity); effects on longer reasoning chains unexplored
